name: Koshoy-Korgon Fortress
full: Koshoy-Korgon fortress site and the Koshoy-Korgon archaeological and ethnographic museum
near: Kara-Suu village — the fortress is about 2 km southeast (eurasia.travel); access via village streets (Lonely Planet: 800 m along the eastern Kyocher street, then left on Abit street). At-Bashy village — about 12–15 km (ilovekg, Journal of Nomads, eurasia.travel); the town of Naryn — about an hour's drive. Note: ilovekg wrongly says “12 km west of Naryn”.
elev: About 2100 m (Nomad's Land — 2107 m). eurasia.travel mentions a “plateau at 2500 m” — that describes the surroundings, not the site itself.
short: Koshoy-Korgon is a medieval fortress town (7th/8th–12th centuries, capital of medieval At-Bashy) with mud-brick walls 245–250 m on each side near the village of Kara-Suu, and a small archaeological and ethnographic museum at the entrance; it is on the UNESCO Tentative List.
desc: The rectangular fortress, 245–250 m across, is surrounded by walls of mud brick and long brick: 7–9 m thick at the base, with a surviving height of 4–8 m (Nomad's Land; up to 10 m according to eurasia.travel). Dozens of towers can be traced along the walls (Nomad's Land counts 60, eurasia.travel about 50), along with a moat 11–14 m wide. The site has been inhabited since at least the 8th century, flourished in the 9th–12th centuries, and its main citadel dates to the Karakhanid era (12th century); it is seen as the medieval town of At-Bash on the Silk Road between Kashgar and Naryn. By the western wall are the remains of a minaret, and in the south are excavations linked to the ruler's residence. According to legend, the fortress was built by Koshoy, a companion and adviser of Manas. The site is on the UNESCO Tentative List (“Nomadic Monuments of the Inner Tian Shan”). At the entrance is a museum built in 2007 with the support of the Dordoi association (gallery since 2010): finds from Koshoy-Korgon and other sites of Naryn region, ethnography and an art collection.
guide: Walk the path along the crest of the old ramparts — it's the best way to grasp the scale: a square of almost 250 by 250 meters with towers around the perimeter. On the west side look for the remains of the minaret, and in the south for the excavations where, according to tradition, the ruler's house stood. Locals link the fortress with Koshoy, Manas's uncle and adviser, although archaeologists date it to the 8th–12th centuries. The museum at the entrance opens irregularly — call or ask the caretaker in Kara-Suu in advance. The best light is at dawn or in the evening: there's no shade in the daytime, so bring water and a hat.
see: Mud-brick walls and towers around the perimeter (245–250 m); the path along the crest of the ramparts; the remains of the minaret by the western wall; excavations by the southern wall; the moat; the Koshoy-Korgon museum at the entrance (artifacts of Naryn region, weapons, utensils, clothing, an art gallery).
skip: You expect a restored fortress like Tash-Rabat — here there are weathered earthen ramparts, interesting more for their scale and history. The museum matters to you and you couldn't arrange for it to be opened. You don't like short stops — it takes only 60–90 minutes in all.
diff: Easy: you can drive almost to the entrance, and the walk over level ground and the ramparts takes 60–90 minutes (ilovekg).
when: May to October; in summer it's hot and shadeless, and after rain the dirt access road turns to mud (ilovekg). In winter the site is accessible, but it is cold and snowy.
hours: The fortress grounds are open, with no fenced entrance. Museum: no regular schedule, “opens rarely” — call or look for the caretaker in advance (ilovekg, Lonely Planet, tury.ru).
daytime: Dawn or evening — soft light on the ramparts and less heat; there's no shade in the daytime (ilovekg).
how: From Naryn along the Naryn — Torugart highway to km 409, at the village of Kara-Suu turn off (about 3 km from the highway — Lonely Planet), then along Kyocher and Abit streets to the fortress. From Naryn it's about an hour's drive (Journal of Nomads). It's easy to combine with a trip to Tash-Rabat — it's the same road.
needcar: Yes: car/taxi from Naryn or At-Bashy; public transport doesn't run for the last kilometers (ilovekg).
self: Yes: no permit needed, the site is open; for the museum, arrange it in advance.
roadtype: The paved Naryn — Torugart highway, then about 3 km through the village and a dirt/gravel road to the fortress (muddy after rain — ilovekg).
traveltime: Naryn — Koshoy-Korgon about 1 h (Journal of Nomads); from At-Bashy 15–20 min (calculated, 12–15 km); Bishkek — Naryn ~5–6 h.
stay: There is no accommodation at the fortress. Options are guesthouses in At-Bashy and Naryn (CBT Naryn), and yurt camps near Tash-Rabat (1500–2000 som/person with breakfast and dinner — snoezelsontheroad, 2025–2026).
net: Not confirmed by operator coverage maps; the village of Kara-Suu and the Torugart highway are nearby, so there is probably a mobile signal (not verified).
entry: The fortress grounds are free (no fenced ticket office). The museum ticket price is not given in the sources (Lonely Planet: “no admission price listed”) — ask the caretaker.
transfer: Not confirmed: taxi prices Naryn — Koshoy-Korgon were not found in the sources. Marshrutka (minibus) Bishkek — Naryn — 600 som (CBT Naryn, 05.2026).
bring: Water, a hat and sunscreen (no shade — ilovekg); comfortable shoes for walking on the ramparts; cash for the museum; the caretaker's number/an arrangement for your visit.
warn: The museum opens irregularly — without calling ahead you may see only the ramparts. Don't climb on crumbling sections of the walls and don't dig or take pottery — this is an archaeological monument (UNESCO Tentative List). The access road turns to mud after rain.
food: No cafe was found at the fortress; eat in At-Bashy or Naryn. Traditional dishes in the Naryn region are beshbarmak, shorpo and kumys (editorial).
reviews: Google Maps: 4.5/5, 106 ratings (as of 03.10.2026, catalog check). Lonely Planet lists the site among the attractions of Naryn region. Pros: the scale of the ramparts, the path along the walls, the link to the Manas epic; cons: the closed museum, few surviving structures, no shade.
p.sum: Koshoy-Korgon is a short stop on the way Naryn → Tash-Rabat/Kel-Suu: about 1 h from Naryn, 15–20 min from At-Bashy. No permit needed. On the Naryn — Torugart highway at the village of Kara-Suu, turn left after the mosque and memorial and drive to the end of the street (≈2–3 km) — the ramparts are in a field on the right, with a private museum next to them (the caretaker speaks Russian/Kyrgyz, the museum costs extra). 30–60 min is enough to look around; stay overnight in At-Bashy or in the yurts at Tash-Rabat.

p.iti.1.plan: Naryn → Koshoy-Korgon → Tash-Rabat (overnight) → Chatyr-Kol; or Naryn → Koshoy-Korgon → At-Bashy → Kyndy → Kel-Suu.
p.season: Year-round; in spring and autumn the access road is muddy after rain; in winter there is snow and the museum is most likely closed; summer is dusty and hot in the daytime.
p.budget.economy: ≈1500–2500 som/person: marshrutka Bishkek—Naryn 600, shared taxi Naryn—At-Bashy + taxi to the fortress, museum (on the spot), a night in a guesthouse ~1400 with breakfast (2021).
p.budget.comfort: A car with driver from Naryn combined with Tash-Rabat + Sandyk hotel $48–54
p.permits: No permit needed (Kara-Suu/At-Bashy are outside the border zone; a permit is required further on — toward Kel-Suu, Chatyr-Kol, Arpa). No fee for the grounds; the museum — a separate fee paid to the caretaker.
p.access: Easy with children and older people (level field, you can drive almost to the ramparts). A stroller — hard going on the dirt, and not possible on the ramparts. Dogs — allowed.
